title: Bar Kokhba (132–135 CE)
hook: a second revolt is crushed, and Jews are barred from Jerusalem

segments.voice: Yesterday, Berakhot, and a table that took the altar's place. Your line was it's who has a seat. Today, a second revolt against Rome, and a hope that rose very high.

"There shall step forth a star out of Jacob." That's a line from the book of Numbers, spoken by Balaam, a promise of a ruler rising from Israel. Years after the Temple burned, a new Jewish commander rose up against Rome, and Rabbi Akiva, a teacher honored by the sages, looked at him and reached for that verse. His name was Koziba, and Akiva read it into the verse: not a star, but Koziba, steps forth out of Jacob. When he saw the man, Akiva said: this is the king, the anointed one. The fighter became known as Bar Kokhba, son of a star.
screen: `"A STAR OUT OF JACOB."` → `AKIVA POINTS TO A COMMANDER.` → `SON OF A STAR.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Jerusalem Talmud, in tractate Taanit. Not everyone agreed with Akiva. Another sage, Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta, answered with a sharp, sad line, in paraphrase: Akiva, grass will grow out of your cheeks, and the son of David still won't have come. You'll be long buried before the redemption arrives, and this isn't it. The revolt was crushed. The Mishnah, in the same list of grief we met with the Temple's fall, records that on the ninth of Av the fortress of Betar was captured. Rome made Jerusalem a Roman city with a new name, Aelia Capitolina, and Jews were barred from entering it. Other rabbinic passages call the commander Bar Koziba, and some readers hear in it son of a lie, a bitter play on the same name. One man, two nicknames, and the gap between them is the story. The rabbis didn't hide that their honored teacher backed a hope that failed. They kept Akiva's words and Yochanan ben Torta's answer side by side, the way they kept Hillel and Shammai, and the page leaves a question for whoever reads it: what do you do with a hope that failed?
screen: `GRASS WILL GROW FROM YOUR CHEEKS.` · `BETAR FALLS ON THE NINTH OF AV.` · then, large: `SON OF A STAR, SON OF A LIE.` · then: `THE RABBIS KEEP THE MISTAKE.`

segments.voice: Let one hope come back to you that didn't come true: a plan, a person you trusted, a cause you were sure of. Say plainly, inside, this didn't work, with no reason and no lesson yet, and notice that you are still here, still breathing, after it. As the week closes, look back too: a wall, two schools, a fall, a fortress, a coffin, a table. If you pray, you can bring the hope that failed to God.
Bar Kokhba. Son of a star, Akiva called him; the revolt was crushed, Betar fell, and Jews were barred from Jerusalem. The rabbis kept the hope and the failure on the record.
Your line: after the revolt. Akiva's words are still there, and so is the answer that told him he was wrong. Day nine hundred three, and a week complete.

howItsDone: The fall of Betar is remembered on Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, alongside the destruction of both Temples, in the fast and the readings of the day.

chat.says: Rabbi Akiva was wrong about Bar Kokhba. Why did the rabbis keep his words?
options: They kept his hope and the answer that he was wrong side by side, honestly.
They changed the story so Akiva never really backed the revolt.
They kept them because Bar Kokhba's revolt actually won.
